(1) Kähler-Meyer 1963/64 'Töne und Akzente in der Formenlehre des Chasu', Afrika und Übersee 47:89-133 (two duplicate Glottolog records, 84552/176698, already in our bibliography) is the direct sequel to the 1962 tonal study and the single most likely source to refine the catalog's stress/tone statement for Chasu; it is print-only (HathiTrust Bd.47-48 umn.31951001892726b search-only, not on archive.org, no DOI) -> priority high. new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Chasu 'tonal' on Kotz 1909 (penultimate 'Ton' plus lexical pitch distinctions) with Hyman 2006 secondary. Philippson confirms the tonal classification from first-hand data and adds an explicit, typologically framed statement that the penult bears a demarcative intensity/length prominence without pitch culmination: compatible with Kotz's 'Der Ton liegt meistens auf der vorletzten Silbe' read as penultimate stress alongside lexical tone; adds detail (four noun-stem tone classes, no length contrast, no Meeussen's rule, N vs S dialect difference in H association).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Asu (Chasu/Pare) is a tone language: four lexical tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems (LL, HL, LH, HH), H vs toneless verb radicals, one-to-one tone-to-syllable association, no Meeussen's rule, no vowel-length contrast; independently of tone, the penultimate syllable of the word carries a non-distinctive intensity accent realized as lengthening (a culmination of length, not of pitch).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect note only: in the southern dialects the H of a verb radical also associates to the extensions (Annexe item 9; ch.4 §3.1); a final H is clearly lowered after a preceding H (p.485). No exceptions to the penultimate length culmination are stated for Asu.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Asu data are his own field notes, examples 'pris dans un sous-dialecte septentrional' (North Pare), with remarks on the southern dialects (H of the radical spreading to extensions); Kähler-Meyer's article concerns Chasu of the Pare mountains (Tanganyika) generally; the catalog record rests on Kotz 1909 (Pare-Gebirge).

tone_statements.quote: Tone Assignment Chasu is inherently a tonal language with two levels of tone (high and low tone) assigned to vowels and syllabic nasals. The words borrowed from non-tonal language are assigned tones as a means of incorporating them into Chasu’s native vocabulary, as well as conforming to the language’s tonal system. As pointed out earlier, since the majority of words are borrowed from Swahili, which by its nature is non-tonal, all loanwords (except the adopted ones) are assigned various tones as illustrated in examples (5a–d). ... It is important to note that since the language has two tones, only high tone is marked. This also applies to loanwords adapted via tone assignment.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Tone Assignment', p.35 (first sentence) and p.36 (last paragraph before 'Substitution (Transphonemization)')
tone_statements.summary: Two-level (H vs L) lexical tone on vowels and syllabic nasals, H marked; tonal minimal pairs incl. loan vs native-meaning doublets.

tone_statements.quote: The tonal pattern of Gonja verbs excluding compound tense was studied according to the tonal classes of the infinitives. It turned out that each tonal pattern was represented by the high level tone, the low level tone and the downstep and that it was derived from two basic (underlying) tones (high and low) and a particular sequence of tones which causes the downstep. ... The unit carrying a tone among segments is called tone bearing unit (TBU). The TBU of the Gonja dialect is a vowel and a syllabic nasal

tone_statements.citation: Herman, Rebecca. 1996. Final Lowering in Kipare. Phonology 13(2): 171-196. doi:10.1017/s0952675700002098
tone_statements.quote: Kipare is a Bantu language which has both lexical tone and final lowering. It has been observed to have lowering of high tones to downstepped highs utterance-finally, lowering of downstepped high tones to lows utterance finally (Odden, 1986 a and b), and lowering of lows to a lower value utterance-finally (Odden, personal communication). [p. 38] ... not only does the phenomenon of final-lowering occur in this Kipare speaker's speech, but also all three tonal categories show final lowering. [p. 40] ... All tonal categories lower, but do not coincide with the next category down. This does not accord with the prediction of the register model. The final tones do seem to be a constant proportion of preceding tones, which does match the prediction of the boundary tone model. The effects of final lowering are non-local, affecting more than just the extreme final tone-bearing unit. [pp. 50-51]

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators (Kotz 1909 p. 3 + Nachtrag p. 73; Hyman 2006:247 ex. 24 + fn. 9). (2) The record rests on a 1909 missionary grammar sketch plus a second-hand report of Kähler-Meyer 1962; that is thin sourcing for a language with a dozen dedicated tonal studies, but every better source opened now agrees with the classification: Kagaya 1989 (Gonja and Mbaga Chasu: two basic tones H/L plus downstep, TBU = vowel/syllabic nasal, no stress section), Schlindwein 1985 (lexical H/L verb radicals, downstep), Herman 1995 (instrumental: three tonal categories H, !H, L; utterance-final lowering), Odden's 1985 précis in the same SAL volume (downstep, utterance-final H register lowering). None mentions an independent word-stress rule; the utterance-final tonal effects are consistent with the phrase domain coded. Languoid identity is sound: Kaga

sources.quote: 'This paper deals with some selected aspects of the tone system of one dialect of Kipare, an Eastern Bantu language spoken in Tanzania. Kipare downstep is the phonetic realization of a floating low tone sandwiched between two high tones ... The Kipare verb radical generally consists of either one or two syllables, the first of which is lexically specified for either a high (H) or a low (L) tone.' No stress/accent/penult statement. (Same volume, Odden's tone-register précis, the text layer: Kipare has downstep but no downdrift and 'a rule assigning an utterance-final H to a lower regist
sources.note: Short open tonal précis (lexical H/L verb radicals, downstep from floating L); independent confirmation of the tonal classification.

All tonal categories lower, but do not coincide with the next category down. This does not accord with the prediction of the register model. The final tones do seem to be a constant proportion of preceding tones, which does match the prediction of the boundary tone model. The effects of final lowering are non-local, affecting more than just the extreme final tone-bearing unit. [pp. 50-51]
